title: Hydraulic Accumulator

introduction.definition: A hydraulic accumulator stores energy as compressed gas. In a bladder accumulator, a rubber bladder inside a steel shell is pre-charged with nitrogen. When system pressure rises above the pre-charge, oil flows in and compresses the gas; when pressure falls, the gas pushes the oil back out. A poppet valve at the oil port stops the bladder being extruded.
applications: Supplementing pump flow for short peaks
Compensating for thermal expansion and leakage
key_points: Pre-charge with NITROGEN only — never oxygen or air
Bladder type: pre-charge ≈ 0.9 × minimum system pressure (rule of thumb)
Gas law sets usable volume (p·Vⁿ = constant)
introduction.summary: A hydraulic accumulator stores energy in compressed gas. In this bladder type a nitrogen-filled bladder sits inside a steel shell; when system pressure rises, oil enters and squeezes the bladder; when pressure falls, the gas pushes the oil back out. Used for energy storage, pulsation damping and emergency power.

working_principle.characteristic_curve: Usable volume ΔV = V₀·(p₀/p₁)^(1/n) − V₀·(p₀/p₂)^(1/n) (n = 1 isothermal, ≈ 1.4 adiabatic).

pressure.title: Gas and oil at the same pressure
pressure.description: The bladder separates nitrogen from oil but transmits pressure, so gas and oil are always at the same pressure. Before any oil enters, the gas is at the pre-charge pressure p₀ (bladder type: typically about 90 % of the minimum system pressure). Oil enters as the system pressure rises, compressing the gas (p·V = constant for slow, isothermal changes; p·V^1.4 for fast, adiabatic ones). The usable oil volume is the gas volume change between maximum and minimum system pressure.

foundation: Mount vertically (gas valve up for bladder type) with clamps that do not restrict the shell; allow access to the gas valve.
alignment: Align motor and pump with the bell housing and coupling; mount cylinders so the rod is not side-loaded (use spherical bearings/clevises).
piping: Fit a safety block with isolation, bleed-down valve and relief valve.
commissioning: Fill through a filter with the specified oil; flush the system to the target cleanliness (ISO 4406 code).
Bleed air; start with relief valves backed off, then set pressures; check for leaks, temperatures and noise.

safety: Always discharge the oil side before any work; an accumulator keeps the system pressurised after the pump stops.

video_tutorials.title: Hydraulic Accumulator — Introduction

script.narration: This module introduces the Hydraulic Accumulator.
A hydraulic accumulator stores energy as compressed gas.
In a bladder accumulator, a rubber bladder inside a steel shell is pre-charged with nitrogen.
When system pressure rises above the pre-charge, oil flows in and compresses the gas; when pressure falls, the gas pushes the oil back out.

Typical applications include emergency/backup energy (e.g. closing valves, braking); supplementing pump flow for short peaks; absorbing pressure shocks and pulsations; compensating for thermal expansion and leakage.
The cutaway reveals the internal construction.
The exploded view separates every component so each one can be tapped for its function, material and failure modes.

script.narration: How the Hydraulic Accumulator works.
The bladder is pre-charged with nitrogen through the gas valve.
System pressure rises; oil enters through the poppet port.
Oil compresses the bladder and gas.
When the system needs flow, gas pressure pushes the oil back out.

The bladder separates nitrogen from oil but transmits pressure, so gas and oil are always at the same pressure.

video_tutorials.title: Hydraulic Accumulator — Maintenance

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Hydraulic Accumulator.
Check system pressure behaviour (pump cycling).
Check pre-charge with a charging kit (oil side drained).
Replace bladder; periodic pressure-vessel inspection per regulations.
Watch for loss of pre-charge: pump cycles more often, poor damping. Common cause: gas valve leak, bladder permeation.
Watch for bladder rupture: gas in oil, no accumulator effect. Common cause: over-compression (pre-charge too low), age.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.
